citeAs: Clark, C., Lee, K., Chang, M.-W., Kwiatkowski, T., Collins, M., and Toutanova, K. (2019). BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions. NAACL 2019.
creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova (Google AI Language, University of Washington)
description: BoolQ (Boolean Questions) is a reading comprehension dataset of 16,000 naturally occurring yes/no questions. Each example consists of a question gathered from anonymized Google search queries, a paragraph from a Wikipedia article containing the answer, the article title, and a yes/no answer label. The dataset is split into a 9.4k train set, 3.2k dev set, and 3.2k test set.
name: BoolQ
rai:annotationsPerItem: 1 (singly-annotated; the paper states "we elected to use singly-annotated examples in the training/dev/test sets in order to be able to gather a larger dataset")
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Three of the authors labelled 110 randomly chosen examples to assess annotation quality. Where there was disagreement, the authors conferred and selected a single answer by mutual agreement, creating "gold-standard" labels. The answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to the gold-standard labels. Of the cases where annotations differed from gold-standard, six were ambiguous or debatable cases, and five were errors where the annotator misunderstood the passage.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators labeled question/article pairs in a three-step process: (1) They decided if the question is "good" — meaning comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information — before seeing the Wikipedia page. (2) For good questions, annotators found a passage within the document containing enough information to answer the question; questions could be marked "not answerable" if the Wikipedia article lacked the information. (3) Annotators marked whether the question's answer is "yes" or "no". Examples were singly annotated (one annotation per item) to allow gathering a larger dataset, after annotation quality was assessed to be sufficiently high (90% accuracy vs. gold-standard labels).
rai:dataBiases: The dataset has a class imbalance: "Yes" answers are slightly more common (62.31% in the train set). The paper notes a correlation between question topic/type and the likelihood of a "yes" answer, though this correlation is too weak to outperform the majority baseline. Questions are sourced from Google search queries, which may reflect biases in what users search for. The dataset is Wikipedia-based, which may introduce domain-specific biases.
rai:dataCollection: Questions were gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries likely to be yes/no questions were heuristically identified by selecting queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words (e.g., "did", "do", "does", "is", "are", "was", "were", "have", "has", "can", "could", "will", "would") and are of sufficient length. Questions were only kept if a Wikipedia page was returned as one of the first five results. The pipeline follows the Natural Questions (NQ) data collection method, with an additional filtering step to focus on yes/no questions. 13k questions were gathered from this pipeline and combined with 3k yes/no questions from the NQ training set, totaling 16k questions.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine paired with Wikipedia pages returned as top search results. Additionally, 3k yes/no questions from the Natural Questions (NQ) training set were incorporated.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web API, Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset has a class imbalance with 62.31% "yes" answers. The question categorization analysis may be slightly out-of-date as the dataset was updated after the analysis was carried out. The dataset is limited to yes/no questions and Wikipedia passages, which may not generalize to other domains. The paper notes that building a document-level version of the task would increase difficulty and correspondence to end-user applications.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions were heuristically filtered to focus on yes/no questions by selecting queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufficient length. Questions were only kept if a Wikipedia page was returned as one of the first five search results. Each question was paired with a selected passage (rather than the entire Wikipedia document) to reduce ambiguity and keep input size manageable. Questions marked as "not answerable" or not "good" were excluded.
rai:dataSocialImpact: BoolQ is directly related to the practical end-task of answering user yes/no questions, making it relevant to real-world question answering applications. The dataset demonstrates that naturally occurring yes/no questions are highly challenging even for state-of-the-art models (best model: 80.4% vs. 90% human accuracy), highlighting a significant gap for future work in natural language understanding.
rai:dataUseCases: Reading comprehension and yes/no question answering; testing models' ability to make complex inferences from text; benchmarking natural language understanding systems; transfer learning research for NLP tasks including entailment and question answering.
